blocks.text: [III, 280] Others interpret the passage of Solomon quite differently. The Greeks: Ἀβασίλευτόν ἐστιν ἡ ἀκρὶς, καὶ ἐκστρατεύει ἀφ᾽ ἑνὸς κελεύσματος εὐτάκτως [Abasileuton estin hē akris, kai ekstrateuei aph᾽ henos keleusmatos eutaktōs]. The Chaldee: The locusts, which have no king, are all gathered together at once, מתכנשין כלהון כחדא. So also the Syriac. And Jerome: The whole goes forth by its bands. And the Arabic: بعسكره امره واخذه بحسن ترتيب [bi-ʿaskarihi amruhu wa-akhdhuhu bi-ḥusn tartīb] In its camp is its affair, and its manner is with fine arrangement. To reconcile these ancient versions either with one another or with the Hebrew text would be very difficult. Yet Aben Ezra, coming close to the Chaldee, renders the Hebrew words ויצא חוצץ as יצא מאוסף ומקובץ, It goes out collected and gathered together. He tries to prove that חצץ is taken in this sense from the words of Job חדשיו חוצצו, that is, he says, נקבעו ונאספו, His months are gathered and collected. But we have shown that that passage must be rendered otherwise. And we deny that the Hebrew חצץ is used anywhere in this way. For Kimchi, in this passage חצץ means to divide herbs and the leaves of trees by cutting them off, so that the sense is: "The locusts have no king, yet they all go out to divide, that is, to cut off, leaves and herbs." In this version there are two things I find wanting. 1. These statements are ἀνακόλουθα [anakolouthа]. For why should locusts not feed and crop the grass even without a king? 2. חצץ does indeed mean to divide, as we have said, but not to cut off. Therefore a certain exceedingly learned man ^{(11)}, who was not pleased with these interpretations, devised another: namely, that חוצץ is derived from the noun חץ, that is, arrow, as in Iud. III, 11. מחצצים, archers; and he explains the passage thus: The locusts have no king, yet they all go forth shooting arrows: that is (he says), darting themselves like arrows. But the Hebrew verb does not mean to shoot arrows; nor is it true, as he supposes, that to shoot arrows is the same as to dart oneself like arrows. Moreover, the flight of locusts is too slow to be compared with an arrow once shot. Finally, these do not [col. 460] cohere well enough: The locusts have no king, yet they all dart themselves like arrows. For birds do not need a king in order to fly swiftly. But he again supposes something further, namely that to dart oneself is the same as to wage war: which I would grant him far less than the earlier points.

If against Solomon's saying that locusts have no king one sets that statement of the Arabs about locusts in Damir, وهو من الحيوان الذي ينقاد لرئيسه فيجتمع كالعسكر اذا ظعن اوله تتابع جميعه [wa-huwa min al-ḥayawān alladhī yanqādu li-raʾīsihi fa-yajtamiʿu ka-l-ʿaskar idhā ẓaʿana awwaluhu tatābaʿa jamīʿuhu] [III, 281] جميعة ظاعنا واذا نزل اوله نزل جميعـه [jamīʿuhu ẓāʿinan wa-idhā nazala awwaluhu nazala jamīʿuhu] It is an animal of the kind that follows a leader and gathers like an army. For when the first of them departs, all follow and likewise depart. And when the first lodges, all the rest lodge too: I answer that the first locust, which the rest follow, is not regarded as a king, such as among bees is اليعسوب [al-yaʿsūb] ὁ ἐσσήν [ho essēn]. For among locusts the one that leads has not been chosen by tacit consent; rather, any one at all, as chance has it, departs or lodges first. To lodge in Arabic is نزل [nazala], that is, to descend onto a field so as to settle there for a time and be refreshed by feeding, as in an inn. In Greek you would say καταλύειν [katalyein]. Hence the son of Sirach says of snow, Ecclesiast. XLIII, 17. (var. 19.), Ὡς ἀκρὶς καταλύουσα ἡ κατάβασις αὐτῆς [Hōs akris katalyousa hē katabasis autēs]· Its descent is like a locust that lodges ^{(12)}.
